notes.b: Sport is big business, and money flows into it in several different ways. Each way has its own name, and the exam expects you to define them separately.
points: Sponsorship: a business provides money, products or services to a sport, team, event or performer in return for association (being linked with it in the public mind), exposure and commercial benefit (a gain in sales or profit).

Title sponsorship: the sponsor's name is attached to a competition, such as the Guinness Six Nations, the men's rugby championship that Guinness has sponsored since 2019. It is also an example of alcohol sponsorship in sport.
Other sponsorship forms: a logo on a team's jersey, and naming rights (the right to put the sponsor's name on a venue or competition).
Endorsement: a performer is paid to publicly promote and use a product or brand (the name and identity a company sells under).
Merchandising: selling branded goods, such as jerseys, scarves, equipment and souvenirs, connected with a sport, team, event or performer.
Sport-related advertising: advertising that uses sport, sports settings or athletes to sell products, including products unrelated to sport.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to define sponsorship and endorsement, and to explain sponsorship, merchandising and sport-related advertising. Keep sponsorship and endorsement distinct: sponsorship is a business relationship with a sport, team or event, while endorsement is a performer promoting a product.

notes.b: The three are easy to mix up because all involve a brand and sport. The difference is who has the relationship and who receives the income.
points: Sponsorship is a business relationship with a sport, team or event, and the income goes to that organisation.
Endorsement is a performer promoting a product, and the income goes to the performer.
Merchandising is the sale of branded goods, and the income goes to the club, NGB (national governing body, the organisation that runs a sport nationally) or event that owns the brand.
Endorsement example: a performer is paid to appear in an advert for a brand of running shoes they wear.
Merchandising example: a club sells replica jerseys and scarves in its shop, and each sale brings income to the club.
notes.tip: A question may ask for the difference between merchandising and endorsement with examples. State who earns the income in each case and give one example of each.

notes.b: A business only sponsors sport if it gets something back. The benefits explain why companies pay, and why sport can rely on them.
points: Brand awareness and exposure to a large audience, because crowds, television viewers and online followers all see the sponsor's name.
A positive image through association with success and with health, because the brand is linked in people's minds with winning teams and fit athletes.
Access to target markets (the groups of customers the business wants to reach), such as the young people and families who follow a sport.
Hospitality for clients and staff at matches and events, such as tickets and entertainment, which builds business relationships.
Higher sales of the sponsor's products, which is the final commercial benefit of the other four.

notes.h: Impact of sponsorship, endorsement and merchandising on sport and performers
notes.b: Each type of commercial deal changes sport and the people in it, for better and for worse. Take them one at a time.
points: Sponsorship funds grassroots programmes (sport for local clubs and beginners), facilities, coaching, events and broadcasting (getting matches onto television and online).
Sponsorship allows elite athletes (those competing at the top level) to train full-time, because the money replaces income from another job.
Endorsement brings large income to star performers and raises their profile.
Endorsement obligations, such as personal appearances and filming, take time away from training.
A performer's image is tied to the brand, so a problem with the brand can damage the performer's reputation, and the reverse.
Merchandising brings major income to clubs and NGBs.
Merchandising builds fan identity with a team, a sport or an event, because fans who wear the kit feel they belong to it.
Replica kits (copies of the team's playing jersey) change often and are expensive for families.
notes.tip: You may be asked to discuss the impact of merchandising on sport. Give both sides: major income and fan identity, against kits that change often and cost families a lot.

notes.h: Sponsorship for the national governing body (NGB): advantages
notes.b: An NGB runs its sport nationally, organising competitions, development and the national teams. It needs money to do this, and sponsors supply a good deal of it.
points: Income: sponsorship money pays for development programmes (bringing new players into the sport) and high-performance programmes (preparing top athletes for elite competition).
Facilities: sponsor funds can build or improve facilities, so the NGB does not have to find that money elsewhere.
Coach education: sponsor funds pay for the training of coaches, so standards of coaching can improve.
Expertise: sponsors bring marketing expertise (skill in promoting and selling) that helps the NGB promote the sport.
Recognition: the NGB's name and competitions gain public recognition through sponsors' advertising.
notes.tip: Questions ask for the advantages of sponsorship for the NGB, and for the impact on a named NGB. Give the advantages for the NGB itself, not for the performer or the sport.

notes.h: Sponsorship for the national governing body (NGB): disadvantages
notes.b: Sponsorship money comes with strings. For an NGB the risks are mainly about depending on the sponsor and about who the sponsor is.
points: Dependence: relying on one sponsor leaves the NGB exposed, because the whole budget rests on one company.
Withdrawal: the NGB loses income if the sponsor withdraws, so programmes it paid for may have to stop.
Influence: a sponsor may try to influence scheduling (when matches are played) and decisions.
Reputation: an unsuitable sponsor can damage the NGB's reputation.
Ethics: brands such as alcohol or gambling can conflict with the values the NGB promotes to young members.

notes.b: For an individual athlete, sponsorship can decide whether a sporting career is affordable. Answer these separately from the NGB and the sport.
points: Income: sponsorship money lets the performer train full-time.
Equipment and travel: sponsors may provide free equipment and travel, which removes costs the athlete would otherwise pay.
Profile: a higher profile can open a career after sport, because the performer is already known to the public and to businesses.
notes.tip: Exam questions name one stakeholder, so give advantages and disadvantages for the performer on their own. Expect to be asked for the positive impact of sponsorship deals for an athlete and for the disadvantages for an athlete.

notes.b: A sponsorship deal is a contract, and the performer has to keep their side of it. That creates several pressures.
points: Obligations: contracts set appearances, filming and other demands on the performer's time.
Pressure: the performer must perform and win to keep the deal.
Injury or poor form: the deal can end after an injury or a run of poor results, because the sponsor's benefit depends on a successful athlete.
Privacy: the performer gives up some privacy when their image is used commercially, because the sponsor wants them seen.
Conduct: the performer must not do anything that damages the brand.
Conflict: the performer's personal deal can clash with the sponsorship of their team, for example if the two sponsors are rivals.
Unwanted products: the performer may be linked to a product they would not choose.

notes.h: Sponsorship for the sport or activity: advantages and disadvantages
notes.b: Here the question is about the sport as a whole, not the NGB or any one athlete. Sponsorship raises a sport's profile, but it can also change it.
points: Advantage, profile: sponsorship brings higher profile and more media coverage.
Advantage, events: sponsors help to fund better events.
Advantage, facilities: sponsors help to fund better facilities.
Advantage, participation: a higher profile can attract more participants.
Disadvantage, inequality: sponsors favour popular sports, men's sport and elite sport, so other sports struggle to attract money.
Disadvantage, commercialisation (turning the sport into a product to be sold): changes are made to suit sponsors and television rather than the sport's own needs.
Disadvantage, image: the sport's image is linked to unhealthy products.
notes.tip: Give advantages and disadvantages for each of the three stakeholders (NGB, performer, sport) separately, because a question names only one.

notes.b: Advertisers use sport because young people watch it and admire its stars. They reach them through several routes.
points: Television and online adverts featuring athletes.
Social media and influencer content (posts by people with large online followings who promote products).
Shirt and stadium advertising, which is seen by everyone at the ground and on television.
Product placement in sport (a brand deliberately shown within the game or its coverage).
Branded events and competitions.

notes.h: Sport-related advertising: positive messages to young people
notes.b: Sport-related advertising can send young people messages that support taking part in sport.
points: Being active is enjoyable and achievable.
Effort and perseverance pay off.
Role models of diverse backgrounds and abilities show that sport is open to everyone.
Healthy lifestyles are presented as normal.
notes.tip: You may be asked to analyse two forms of sport-related advertising in terms of their messages to young people. Name the form, then give both a positive and a negative message.

notes.h: Sport-related advertising: negative messages to young people
notes.b: The same advertising can also harm young viewers, who are still forming their ideas about health, bodies and success.
points: Sport is linked with unhealthy products such as sugary drinks, fast food, alcohol and gambling.
Unrealistic body ideals are presented as the norm.
Success appears to depend on expensive gear, which can make sport seem out of reach for families who cannot afford it.
Winning at all costs is presented as the goal.
Betting adverts shown during matches normalise gambling, meaning it comes to seem an ordinary part of watching sport.

notes.b: When an exam shows or describes an advert, work through the same five steps in order. They turn a vague impression into marked points.
points: 1. Who is shown: the age, gender, body type and ability of the people in the advert.
2. What product is sold, and whether it is linked to health or to sport.
3. What message the advert gives about sport, bodies and success.
4. Whether that message is positive or negative for young viewers, and why.
5. The likely effect on young viewers: whether it encourages activity, unhealthy choices or unrealistic expectations.

notes.h: Code of practice for selecting sponsors of youth sport
notes.b: A code of practice is a set of rules a club agrees to follow when choosing sponsors. Each criterion below carries a justification, so the committee can explain its choice to parents and members.
points: Criterion 1: no sponsors whose products are unsuitable for young people, such as alcohol, gambling, tobacco and vaping, or high-fat and high-sugar food and drink.
Justification for criterion 1: a logo on a child's jersey is a constant endorsement to the child and everyone watching, so an unhealthy brand contradicts the club's health message.
Criterion 2: the sponsor's values and conduct must match the club's code of ethics, child safeguarding (protecting children from harm), inclusion and fair play.
Justification for criterion 2: a sponsor shown on the club's kit is associated with its values, so a sponsor whose conduct breaks them damages the club's credibility with young players and parents.

Criterion 3: no use of children's images, names or data in marketing without parental consent. Justification: children cannot judge how a commercial company will use their image, so parents must decide.

Criterion 4: sponsorship benefits the whole club fairly, including girls' and boys' teams and all age groups, not only elite teams. Justification: a deal that funds one team alone leaves other young members without coaching, facilities or equipment.

Criterion 5: the sponsor has no say over team selection, coaching or club decisions. Justification: selection and coaching should reflect players' ability and development, not what suits a commercial partner.
Criterion 6: a transparent written agreement, approved by the committee, with a fixed term and a review and exit clause (a condition allowing the club to leave the deal).
Justification for criterion 6: a written, time-limited agreement lets the club check what it receives, review the deal and leave it if the sponsor no longer meets the criteria.
notes.tip: You may be asked to state and justify three criteria for a code of practice for selecting commercial sponsorship for a youth team. Pick three, and give each a justification in the same sentence.

keyTerms.definition: A business's provision of money, products or services to a sport, team, event or performer in return for association, exposure and commercial benefit.
A sponsorship in which the sponsor's name is attached to a competition or event.
The right to attach a sponsor's name to a venue or competition.
A paid arrangement in which a performer publicly promotes and uses a product or brand.
The sale of branded goods connected with a sport, team, event or performer.
Advertising that uses sport, sports settings or athletes to sell products, including products unrelated to sport.
The deliberate display of a brand's product within a sporting event, broadcast or competition.
A social media personality who is paid or sponsored to promote products to their followers.
How widely a brand is known, which sponsorship and advertising aim to increase.
A copy of a team's playing kit sold to supporters.
The growth of sport as a business, with decisions shaped by money and commercial partners.
A set of agreed rules that states the standards an organisation must meet.

questions.prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of sponsorship for a national governing body, the performers and the sport.
questions.model: For the NGB, sponsorship brings income for development and high-performance programmes, funds facilities and coach education, gives access to sponsors' marketing expertise, and raises the sport's profile. The disadvantages are dependence on one sponsor, the loss of income if that sponsor withdraws, the risk that a sponsor influences scheduling and decisions, reputational damage from an unsuitable sponsor, and ethical conflicts with brands such as alcohol or gambling. For the performer, the advantages are income to train full-time, free equipment and travel, and a higher profile that can help a career after sport. The disadvantages are contractual obligations and time demands, pressure to perform and win to keep the deal, the loss of the deal after injury or poor form, reduced privacy, the need to avoid damaging the brand, possible clashes with team sponsors, and being linked to a product they would not choose. For the sport, sponsorship brings higher profile and media coverage, better events and facilities, and more participants. The disadvantages are that sponsors favour popular, men's and elite sport, so other sports struggle to attract money; that commercialisation changes the sport to suit sponsors and television; and that the sport's image becomes linked to unhealthy products.

questions.prompt: Write three statements you would include in a code of practice for selecting commercial sponsorship for a youth sports team, and justify each.
questions.model: 1. No sponsors whose products are unsuitable for young people, such as alcohol, gambling, tobacco and vaping, or high-fat and high-sugar food and drink. Justification: a sponsor's logo on a young player's jersey is a constant endorsement to the player and everyone watching, so an unhealthy brand contradicts the club's health message. 2. The sponsor has no say over team selection, coaching or club decisions. Justification: selection must reflect each player's ability and development, and a sponsor that influenced selection would undermine fair play and the development of every young member. 3. No use of children's images, names or data in marketing without parental consent. Justification: children cannot judge how a company will use their image, so the parents must decide, which protects the child's privacy and safety.

questions.prompt: Analyse two different forms of sport-related advertising in terms of the messages they give to young people.
questions.model: Television and online adverts featuring athletes: a positive message is that effort and perseverance pay off, because the athlete is shown training hard and succeeding, so young viewers learn that persistence brings results. A negative message is that unrealistic body ideals and expensive gear are presented as the route to success, so a young viewer may compare their own body with the athlete's and feel they must buy the product to succeed. Social media and influencer content: a positive message is that role models of diverse backgrounds and abilities show that sport is open to everyone, so young people who doubt themselves see someone like them taking part. A negative message is that influencers promote unhealthy products such as sugary drinks and fast food, linking sport with unhealthy choices, and that the posts can present unrealistic body ideals as normal.
